questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of chemical weathering?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Frost Action**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Frost Action** is a physical weathering process where water enters cracks in rocks, freezes, and expands, causing the rock to fracture and break apart. It does not involve chemical changes, making it a part of physical weathering and not chemical weathering.
 
• **Hydration:** This is a chemical weathering process in which minerals absorb water and undergo chemical changes, often leading to expansion and weakening of the rock. ***Hence, this is a part of chemical weathering.***
 
• **Oxidation:** This chemical weathering process involves the reaction of oxygen with minerals, particularly iron, forming oxides (e.g., rust). It weakens the rock over time. ***Hence, this is a part of chemical weathering.***
 
• **Carbonation:** This is a chemical weathering process where carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which then dissolves minerals like calcium carbonate in rocks such as limestone. ***Hence, this is a part of chemical weathering.***
 
• ***Thus, Frost Action is NOT a part of chemical weathering as it involves physical processes rather than chemical reactions.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Physical Weathering:**

 
 
• Physical weathering involves the breakdown of rocks through mechanical processes such as temperature changes, abrasion, and freeze-thaw cycles.
 
• **Frost Action:** A common physical weathering process, particularly in cold climates, where water freezes inside cracks and expands, breaking the rock apart.
 
• Other processes include thermal expansion, exfoliation, and abrasion caused by wind, water, or glaciers.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Weathering:**
 
 
• Chemical weathering involves the decomposition or alteration of rocks due to chemical reactions between minerals and external agents like water, oxygen, and acids.
 
• **Hydration:** Minerals absorb water, causing structural changes, expansion, and weakening of the rock.
 
• **Oxidation:** Oxygen reacts with iron or other minerals to form oxides, leading to rust formation and weakening of rocks.
 
• **Carbonation:** Carbonic acid dissolves minerals like calcium carbonate, especially in limestone and marble, leading to features like caves and sinkholes.
 
 
 
• **Key Differences Between Physical and Chemical Weathering:**
 
 
• **Physical Weathering:** Does not alter the chemical composition of rocks; examples include frost action and abrasion.
 
• **Chemical Weathering:** Alters the chemical composition of rocks, leading to decomposition; examples include hydration, oxidation, and carbonation.
 
• Both types of weathering work together to break down rocks and form soil over time.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Chemical Weathering:**
 
 
• **Hydration:** Feldspar minerals in granite absorb water and transform into clay minerals.
 
• **Oxidation:** Iron-rich minerals in basalt react with oxygen to form rust.
 
• **Carbonation:** Carbon dioxide in rainwater dissolves limestone, creating caves and karst topography.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Weathering:**

 
 
• Weathering contributes to soil formation, nutrient cycling, and landscape modification.
 
• It can weaken structures like buildings and bridges over time, requiring maintenance and reinforcement.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Weathering Study:**
 
 
• Understanding weathering processes helps in construction planning and selecting materials resistant to weathering.
 
• It assists geologists in studying the history of landscapes and predicting geological hazards like landslides.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Aajeevika - Deendayal Antyodaya YojnaNational Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM) launched by the Ministry of Rural Development (MoRD), Government of India?

The correct answer is __**2011**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Aajeevika - Deendayal Antyodaya Yojna**, also known as the **National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM)**, was launched in **June 2011** by the **Ministry of Rural Development** (MoRD), Government of India.
 
• The mission aims to **create efficient and effective institutional platforms** for the rural poor, enabling them to increase household income and improve their quality of life.
 
• DAY-NRLM was launched as a **flagship program** to reduce poverty by enabling access to gainful employment through skill development, sustainable livelihoods, and opportunities for self-employment.
 
• The program primarily focuses on promoting **women-led self-help groups (SHGs)** and building social capital in rural areas.
 
• The mission targets the **Below Poverty Line (BPL)** population, emphasizing inclusivity and community-driven models for poverty alleviation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Objectives of DAY-NRLM:**

 
 
• The mission aims to **enhance access to financial resources**, including loans, insurance, and savings for rural poor households.
 
• It seeks to promote **sustainable livelihood opportunities** through skill development, entrepreneurship, and market linkages.
 
• The program works to strengthen the **social capital** of rural areas by promoting women-led SHGs, federations, and community networks.
 
 
 
• **Key Features:**
 
 
• Focus on **women empowerment:** At least one woman from each poor household is encouraged to join SHGs.
 
• Implementation is based on the principle of **community participation**, where local organizations play an active role in decision-making.
 
• The program emphasizes **capacity building** for rural communities and institutions to ensure long-term impact.
 
• It uses a **targeted approach** to identify and assist the poorest households across rural India.
 
 
 
• **Achievements:**
 
 
• By 2023, the mission has successfully mobilized over **8 crore households** into SHGs.
 
• It has facilitated access to **credit worth billions** to SHGs, enabling them to start small businesses and improve livelihoods.
 
 
 
• **Other Poverty Alleviation Programs:**
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA):** Provides wage employment opportunities.
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awaas Yojana - Gramin:** Focuses on providing housing for rural poor households.
 
• **National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP):** Offers pensions to elderly, widows, and disabled individuals in rural areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Background:**

 
 
• DAY-NRLM replaced the earlier **Swarna Jayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY)**, which was operational from **1999 to 2011**.
 
• SGSY faced challenges related to targeting beneficiaries and institutional inefficiencies, which led to the need for a revamped program.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• DAY-NRLM aligns with the **United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**, particularly Goal 1 (No Poverty) and Goal 5 (Gender Equality).
 
• The mission contributes to India's efforts to achieve **inclusive growth** and reduce inequality in rural areas.

questions.question: What was the ultimate promise made by Bhagirath Majhi to the Santhals if they followed his teachings?

options.text: Access to modern education and jobs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Land restoration and divine protection**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bhagirath Majhi**, a prominent leader of the **Santhal community**, is remembered for his efforts to unite the Santhals and restore their rights and dignity.
 
• He promised the Santhals the restoration of their **ancestral lands**, which were being exploited and taken away during the British colonial period through oppressive laws and systems like **Zamindari**.
 
• In addition to land restoration, Bhagirath Majhi also sought to provide the Santhals with a sense of **divine protection**. His teachings often intertwined spirituality and resistance, motivating the Santhals to fight against exploitation and injustice.
 
• The promise of land restoration and divine protection was crucial in rallying the Santhals to unite under Bhagirath Majhi's leadership to resist the oppression they faced under the British and local landlords.
 
• This promise of land rights and spiritual assurance resonated deeply with the Santhals, whose lives were closely tied to their ancestral lands and indigenous beliefs, making it a compelling call for resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Santhal Rebellion (1855-1856):**

 
 
• The Santhal Rebellion was one of the early tribal uprisings against British colonial rule and the exploitative practices of landlords and moneylenders.
 
• It was led by **Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand, and Bhairav Murmu**, alongside leaders like Bhagirath Majhi.
 
• The rebellion arose due to the loss of ancestral lands, forced labor, and exploitation under the **Zamindari system**.
 
 
 
• **Land Rights:**
 
 
• For the Santhals, land was not only a source of livelihood but also held spiritual significance, as they believed in living in harmony with nature.
 
• The alienation of tribal lands by British and non-tribal landlords created economic hardships and cultural dislocation for the Santhals.
 
• The promise of land restoration was a key rallying point for tribal uprisings, as it symbolized the return of their dignity and way of life.
 
 
 
• **Religious Beliefs:**
 
 
• Santhals follow a nature-based religion, worshiping **Marang Buru** (Great Spirit) and other deities associated with nature and agriculture.
 
• Bhagirath Majhi's emphasis on divine protection resonated with the Santhals’ spiritual beliefs, further strengthening their resolve to fight against oppression.
 
• The blending of spiritual guidance and political resistance was a unique feature of tribal movements like the one led by Bhagirath Majhi.
 
 
 
• **British Colonial Policies:**
 
 
• The British introduced exploitative revenue systems like the **Zamindari system**, which led to the displacement of tribal communities from their ancestral lands.
 
• Tribal communities were often coerced into bonded labor and subjected to high taxes and debts, leading to widespread poverty.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the High Endurance Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (HEAUV) developed by DRDO’s Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL)?

• It is designed to operate autonomously, enabling it to gather critical data and monitor underwater activities without direct human intervention.
 
• This vehicle plays a vital role in detecting and tracking **submarine movements**, ensuring the security of maritime zones and naval operations.
 
• The HEAUV is equipped with cutting-edge technology, including **sonar systems and sensors**, allowing it to identify underwater objects and threats effectively.
 
• This technology is instrumental in safeguarding India's maritime interests, enhancing **defense capabilities**, and supporting strategic operations in underwater domains.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **High Endurance Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (HEAUV):**

 
 
• Developed by the **Naval Science and Technological Laboratory (NSTL)**, a division of DRDO, specifically for underwater surveillance and reconnaissance.
 
• HEAUV is equipped with **advanced sonar, cameras, navigation systems, and sensors** to perform real-time underwater mapping and detection.
 
• The vehicle is capable of operating for extended durations under the sea, thus ensuring high endurance and efficiency in conducting surveillance missions.
 
 
 
• **Underwater Surveillance Technology:**
 
 
• Underwater surveillance is crucial for monitoring maritime borders, detecting threats, and ensuring **security against enemy submarines**.
 
• Modern surveillance systems rely on **autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs)**, which are unmanned and remotely operated vehicles designed for efficient monitoring tasks.
 
• Such systems are extensively used by naval forces worldwide to protect territorial waters and conduct intelligence operations.
 
 
 
• **DRDO's Role in Maritime Security:**
 
 
• The **Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO)** is India's premier agency for developing advanced defense technology for the armed forces.
 
• DRDO's NSTL specializes in **naval research and development**, focusing on underwater technologies, sonar systems, and torpedoes.
 
• Its innovations, such as the HEAUV, are pivotal in strengthening India's maritime defense capabilities.
 
 
 
• **Applications of HEAUV:**
 
 
• Primarily used for **underwater surveillance** in maritime zones.
 
• Supports naval operations by **detecting enemy submarines** and underwater threats.
 
• Assists in conducting **oceanographic surveys** and underwater research.
 
• Contributes to environmental monitoring and safeguarding underwater ecosystems.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Option 2:** Surface-to-air missile deployment is unrelated to HEAUV, as it is designed for underwater operations.
 
• **Option 3:** Submarine crew training is not the purpose of HEAUV; its focus is on autonomous surveillance.
 
• **Option 4:** Deep-sea oil exploration is a commercial activity and not the intended use of HEAUV.
 
 
 
• The development of HEAUV showcases India's commitment to achieving self-reliance in defense technology and securing its maritime boundaries effectively.

questions.question: Colonial economic policies created a skewed distribution of income and wealth in Indian society. Which of the following is a key indicator of income inequality in colonial India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Unequal land ownership patterns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Unequal land ownership patterns** were one of the most prominent indicators of income inequality in colonial India.
 
• The **British land revenue systems**, such as the **Permanent Settlement** (introduced in 1793) and **Ryotwari system**, created a class of landlords who held vast tracts of land, while the majority of the population consisted of poor tenant farmers or laborers.
 
• Landlords often exploited tenants by charging exorbitant rents, further deepening economic disparities.
 
• The lack of access to land for the majority of the population meant that wealth was concentrated in the hands of a few individuals or families.
 
• This skewed distribution of land ownership perpetuated poverty and reduced economic mobility for a large segment of Indian society during the colonial period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Colonial economic policies:**

 
 
• The British economic policies in India were primarily extractive and exploitative, aimed at benefiting the colonial rulers rather than the Indian population.
 
• These policies included high taxation, forced commercialization of agriculture, and minimal investment in industrial development.
 
• The introduction of the **Permanent Settlement** in Bengal was a pivotal moment in creating a landlord class that held disproportionate wealth and power.
 
 
 
• **Other Indicators of Income Inequality:**
 
 
• The lack of access to education for the majority of the population contributed to income disparities, as literacy and skills were concentrated among the elite.
 
• Unequal wage distribution across sectors, such as agriculture and industrial labor, further exacerbated the economic divide.
 
• Limited irrigation and infrastructure investments in rural areas led to low agricultural productivity, which was a significant contributor to rural poverty.
 
 
 
• **Permanent Settlement System:**
 
 
• Implemented by the British in 1793, this system fixed the land revenue that landlords had to pay to the colonial government.
 
• Landlords were granted ownership rights to vast tracts of land, while tenant farmers had little to no rights and were heavily exploited.
 
 
 
• **Ryotwari System:**
 
 
• In areas like Madras and Bombay, the Ryotwari system allowed direct revenue collection from individual farmers.
 
• However, high taxation rates under this system pushed farmers into poverty and debt.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Impacts of Unequal Land Ownership:**

 
 
• Unequal land ownership patterns led to the concentration of wealth among landlords and systemic poverty among tenant farmers.
 
• Such disparities hindered agricultural development and contributed to frequent famines and food shortages during colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Social Impacts:**
 
 
• Economic inequality reinforced social hierarchies and caste-based discrimination, as land ownership was often tied to caste privilege.
 
• It restricted upward mobility for marginalized communities and perpetuated generational poverty.
 
 
 
• **Post-Independence Reforms:**
 
 
• After independence, land reforms such as land redistribution and abolition of the zamindari system were initiated to address these inequalities.
 
• However, the implementation of these reforms varied across states, and issues of land inequality persist in modern India.

questions.question: What is the total number of inhabited islands in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, as of May 2025?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** consist of a group of 572 islands, out of which a total of **more than 30 islands are inhabited**. These inhabited islands are spread across the two major groups: Andaman and Nicobar.
 
• The islands are divided into two groups: the **Andaman Islands** (located in the north) and the **Nicobar Islands** (located in the south).
 
• Among the inhabited islands, notable ones include **Port Blair** (capital of Andaman and Nicobar Islands), **Havelock Island**, **Neil Island**, and **Car Nicobar**.
 
• The inhabited islands support a population comprising various communities including **indigenous tribes**, settlers from mainland India, and others.
 
• As of the latest data available, the total number of inhabited islands is determined to be **more than 30**, based on government records and population census surveys.

__
 
• **Geography of Andaman and Nicobar Islands:**

 
 
• The islands are located in the **Bay of Bengal**, about 1,200 kilometers from the eastern coast of India.
 
• The group of islands is divided into the **Andaman Islands** (north) and the **Nicobar Islands** (south).
 
• The islands are known for their rich biodiversity, tropical rainforests, coral reefs, and mangroves.
 
 
 
• **Population and Tribal Communities:**
 
 
• The islands are home to both settlers from mainland India and **indigenous tribal communities**.
 
• Prominent tribes include the **Great Andamanese**, **Onges**, **Jarawas**, and **Sentinelese**.
 
• The Nicobar Islands primarily host the Nicobarese tribe and Shompens.
 
 
 
• **Important Islands:**
 
 
• Key inhabited islands in the Andaman group include **Port Blair**, **Havelock Island** (now Swaraj Dweep), and **Neil Island** (now Shaheed Dweep).
 
• Important inhabited islands in the Nicobar group include **Car Nicobar** and **Great Nicobar**.
 
 
 
• **Tourism and Economy:**
 
 
• The islands are popular for tourism activities such as **scuba diving**, **snorkeling**, and exploring pristine beaches.
 
• Economic activities include **agriculture**, **fisheries**, and **forest-based industries**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Biodiversity:**

 
 
• The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are home to a **diverse ecosystem**, including unique flora and fauna.
 
• The islands are part of the **Indo-Malayan biodiversity hotspot**.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Importance:**
 
 
• The islands are strategically important for India in terms of defense and maritime security.
 
• They serve as a crucial base for the **Indian Navy** and **Coast Guard**.
 
 
 
• **Climate:**
 
 
• The islands experience a **tropical monsoon climate** with heavy rainfall.
 
• Severe weather conditions, such as cyclones, occasionally impact the region.

questions.question: Which of the following terms describe a change in the DNA sequence resulting in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mutation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mutation** refers to a permanent alteration in the **DNA sequence** of an organism's genome. This change can occur due to errors during DNA replication or exposure to mutagens such as radiation, chemicals, or viruses.
 
• Mutations can lead to changes in the **genotype** (the genetic makeup) and the **phenotype** (observable characteristics) of an organism, influencing traits such as physical appearance, metabolic functions, or susceptibility to diseases.
 
• There are different types of mutations, such as **point mutations** (substitution of a single nucleotide), **insertions**, **deletions**, and **chromosomal mutations** (affecting large sections of DNA).
 
• Mutations can be beneficial, neutral, or harmful depending on their impact on the organism's ability to survive and reproduce. For example, beneficial mutations contribute to **evolution** and adaptation.
 
• Mutations are crucial in genetics and molecular biology as they serve as the basis for studying hereditary diseases, genetic disorders, and evolutionary processes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Segregation:**

 
 
• **Mendel’s law of segregation** refers to the separation of alleles during gamete formation, ensuring that each gamete carries only one allele from a pair.
 
• It explains why offspring inherit traits from both parents but is unrelated to changes in the DNA sequence. *Hence, this is not correct in the context of the question.*
 
 
 
• **Dominance:**
 
 
• **Dominance** is a genetic principle where one allele masks the expression of another allele in a heterozygous pair.
 
• This concept explains the inheritance pattern of certain traits but does not involve alterations in DNA sequences. *Thus, this option is incorrect for the given question.*
 
 
 
• **Transcription:**
 
 
• **Transcription** is the process by which genetic information encoded in DNA is copied into RNA.
 
• It is a normal cellular process and does not involve permanent changes to the DNA sequence. *Therefore, this option is not relevant to the question.*
 
 
 
• **Impact of Mutations:**
 
 
• Mutations have been extensively studied in genetics to understand diseases such as **sickle cell anemia**, **cystic fibrosis**, and **cancer**, which are caused by genetic changes.
 
• They are also key to **artificial selection** and **genetic engineering**, allowing scientists to alter genomes for research and therapeutic purposes.
 
• Mutations are vital in evolutionary biology, as they provide the genetic variation required for **natural selection**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Types of Mutations:**

 
 
• **Point mutations:** Involve a single nucleotide change. Example: Substitution in sickle cell anemia.
 
• **Insertion or deletion:** Addition or loss of nucleotides in DNA, causing frameshift mutations.
 
• **Chromosomal mutations:** Large-scale changes affecting entire segments of chromosomes. Example: Down syndrome caused by trisomy 21.
 
 
 
• **Causes of Mutations:**
 
 
• Errors during **DNA replication**.
 
• Exposure to **mutagens** like UV radiation, X-rays, and harmful chemicals.
 
• Viral infections that integrate into the host genome.
 
 
 
• **Applications in Science:**
 
 
• Used in **genetic engineering** and **CRISPR** technology to modify organisms.
 
• Study of mutations helps in developing treatments for **genetic disorders**.
 
• Mutations serve as the basis for understanding **evolutionary mechanisms**.

questions.question: Which of the following is the primary objective of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005?

options.text: To promote transparency and accountability in government functioning
To regulate foreign investment in India
To control corruption in the judiciary
To ensure reservations for backwards classes

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To promote transparency and accountability in government functioning**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005** was enacted to foster **transparency and accountability** in the functioning of government bodies.
 
• It empowers citizens to seek information from **public authorities**, ensuring that government processes are open and accessible.
 
• The RTI Act is crucial for **strengthening democracy**, as it enables individuals to participate actively in governance by accessing essential information.
 
• Under the Act, public authorities are required to disclose information proactively and respond to citizens' requests within a specified timeframe. 
 
• It is an effective tool for combating corruption by allowing citizens to scrutinize **decision-making processes** and hold officials accountable for their actions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Features of the RTI Act, 2005:**

 
 
• The Act applies to all levels of government, including **central, state, and local authorities**, as well as non-government organizations receiving government funds.
 
• Every citizen has the right to request information, and public authorities are obligated to provide it within **30 days** of the request.
 
• Public authorities are required to appoint **Public Information Officers (PIOs)** to handle RTI requests efficiently.
 
• Citizens can appeal if their request is denied or if they are dissatisfied with the response, through a **two-tier appeal mechanism**.
 
 
 
• **Role in Promoting Good Governance:**
 
 
• The RTI Act has been instrumental in promoting **transparency, accountability, and participatory governance**.
 
• It ensures informed citizenry, enabling individuals to question inefficiencies and demand better services.
 
• RTI has played a significant role in uncovering **corruption cases** and improving public trust in government institutions.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Options:**
 
 
• Option 2: "To regulate foreign investment in India" is incorrect, as RTI is unrelated to foreign investment. Regulation of foreign investment is primarily governed by **FDI policies and FEMA**.
 
• Option 3: "To control corruption in the judiciary" is incorrect, as RTI focuses on transparency in all governmental functions, not solely on the judiciary.
 
• Option 4: "To ensure reservations for backward classes" is unrelated to RTI. Reservation policies are governed under **Articles 15 and 16** of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Impact of RTI Act:**
 
 
• Since its implementation, RTI has led to significant improvements in **public sector transparency**, especially in areas like infrastructure projects, government schemes, and resource allocation.
 
• It has empowered citizens by providing them access to critical information about **policy decisions, public spending, and administrative actions**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **RTI and Judicial Interpretation:**

 
 
• The Supreme Court of India has repeatedly upheld the importance of RTI in ensuring **citizens' right to information** under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
 
• In several cases, the judiciary has emphasized that the right to information is integral to a **transparent and democratic society**.
 
 
 
• **Exemptions under RTI Act:**
 
 
• Certain sensitive information like **national security, foreign relations, and personal privacy** is exempted under Sections 8 and 9 of the Act.
 
• However, even exempt information can be disclosed if it serves a larger public interest.
 
 
 
• **RTI in Practice:**
 
 
• Since its inception, RTI has been widely used by activists, journalists, and ordinary citizens to demand transparency in government actions.
 
• Some prominent instances include revelations about **large-scale scams** like the Commonwealth Games scam and various public works projects.

questions.question: Rohilla chief, Najib-ud-Daula, played a key role in the ____.

__
 
• **Najib-ud-Daula**, also known as Najib Khan Rohilla, was the chief of the **Rohilla Afghan clan** and played a significant role in the political landscape of Northern India in the mid-18th century.
 
• He was one of the key allies of the **Durrani Empire**, led by **Ahmad Shah Abdali** (also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani), during the **Third Battle of Panipat** in **1761**.
 
• The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on **14 January 1761**, between the Marathas and the Afghan forces under Ahmad Shah Abdali, supported by Najib-ud-Daula and other allies.
 
• Najib-ud-Daula's efforts in organizing the Afghan forces and ensuring the supply of resources were crucial to Abdali's victory over the Marathas in this decisive battle.
 
• His role in the battle marked a turning point in Indian history, as it temporarily halted the expansion of the **Maratha Empire** and reasserted the influence of the Mughal-Afghan alliance in Northern India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Third Battle of Panipat (1761):**

 
 
• The battle took place near **Panipat**, in present-day **Haryana**, India.
 
• It was one of the largest and bloodiest battles fought in the 18th century, involving over **125,000 troops** on both sides.
 
• The Marathas, under the leadership of **Sadashivrao Bhau**, faced a coalition of forces led by **Ahmad Shah Abdali**, who was supported by Najib-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Oudh, and Shuja-ud-Daula.
 
• The defeat of the Marathas in this battle marked the decline of their political power and opened the way for British dominance in India in the following decades.
 
 
 
• **Role of Najib-ud-Daula:**
 
 
• Najib-ud-Daula played a pivotal role in forming the alliance between Ahmad Shah Abdali and other regional powers, including the Nawabs of Oudh and Bengal.
 
• He was instrumental in mobilizing resources and troops for Abdali's campaign against the Marathas.
 
• After the battle, Najib-ud-Daula emerged as a key player in the Mughal court and was appointed as the **Mir Bakshi** (paymaster general) of the Mughal Empire.
 
 
 
• **Other Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Third Battle of Panipat was not just a military conflict but also a cultural and economic turning point in Indian history. It marked the end of the era of large-scale native Indian empires and the beginning of regional fragmentation.
 
• The battle significantly weakened the Marathas, paving the way for the rise of the **British East India Company** in the late 18th century.
 
• The defeat of the Marathas also led to widespread social and economic consequences, including a significant loss of life and disruption in trade and agriculture in Northern India.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The Third Battle of Panipat is remembered as one of the most important battles in Indian history due to its far-reaching consequences on the political and social fabric of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Najib-ud-Daula's alliance with Ahmad Shah Abdali demonstrated the complexities of regional politics during this period, where alliances were often formed based on mutual interests rather than ethnic or religious solidarity.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a key feature of a Public-Private Partnership (PPP)?

options.text: Government and private entities share responsibilities and risks efficiently.
The public partner fully finances a project, while the private partner has no risk.
PPPs are only used for purely social (non-commercial) projects.
Only public sector entities can participate in PPPs.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Government and private entities share responsibilities and risks efficiently.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs)** are collaborative arrangements between the government and private entities to deliver projects or services, sharing responsibilities and risks efficiently.
 
• In a PPP model, the **government** usually provides regulatory oversight, while the **private sector** brings expertise, financing, and operational efficiency.
 
• These partnerships are aimed at **efficiently utilizing resources** from both sectors to address public needs, such as infrastructure development, healthcare, education, and public services.
 
• PPP projects are structured to **share risks** between the public and private partners, ensuring better risk management and project accountability.
 
• Unlike traditional public sector projects, PPPs **engage the private sector** in a way that leverages its innovation and efficiency, while ensuring public welfare goals are met.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Features of PPP:**

 
 
• PPPs are used for **infrastructure projects** like highways, railways, airports, water supply systems, and urban development.
 
• The private sector typically invests in the project and assumes operational risk, while the government ensures regulatory compliance and public interest.
 
• PPPs are governed by **contractual agreements** outlining responsibilities, funding mechanisms, and risk-sharing models.
 
• Examples include **India's National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)** toll roads and **Delhi Metro Airport Express Line**.
 
 
 
• **Statement Analysis:**
 
 
• Statement 1: "Government and private entities share responsibilities and risks efficiently." ***Correct***. This accurately describes the essence of a PPP model.
 
• Statement 2: "The public partner fully finances a project, while the private partner has no risk." ***Incorrect***. PPPs involve shared financial responsibilities and risk allocation between public and private partners.
 
• Statement 3: "PPPs are only used for purely social (non-commercial) projects." ***Incorrect***. PPPs are used for both commercial and social projects, including infrastructure and public services.
 
• Statement 4: "Only public sector entities can participate in PPPs." ***Incorrect***. Private sector entities play a crucial role in PPPs, contributing expertise, innovation, and funding.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **India's PPP Framework:** India follows a robust PPP framework, guided by policies like the **Model Concession Agreement (MCA)** and **Viability Gap Funding (VGF)**.
 
• **Global Examples:** PPPs are widely used internationally, such as the **Crossrail Project in the UK** and **Australia's Sydney Harbour Tunnel**.
 
• **Benefits:** PPPs improve **resource efficiency**, enable **innovation**, and ensure the delivery of high-quality services while maintaining public welfare.

questions.question: Which type of land is most suitable for agriculture in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Level alluvial land**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Level alluvial land** is considered the most suitable type of land for agriculture in India due to its **fertility and nutrient-rich soil composition**.
 
• Alluvial soils are formed by the deposition of **sediments brought by rivers and streams**, making them highly productive for crops.
 
• These soils are extensively found in the **Indo-Gangetic plains**, covering states like Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and West Bengal.
 
• The **fine texture and adequate water-retention capacity** of alluvial soil make it ideal for growing crops like wheat, rice, sugarcane, and cotton.
 
• Alluvial soils are **renewable and self-replenishing** due to regular silt deposition by rivers, ensuring long-term agricultural productivity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mountainous Land**:

 
 
• Mountainous land is characterized by its **rugged terrain** and steep slopes, making it **less suitable** for large-scale agriculture.
 
• However, in regions like the Himalayan foothills, **terrace farming** is practiced to grow crops such as tea, rice, and vegetables.
 
• The soil here is often shallow and prone to erosion, limiting its agricultural potential.
 
 
 
• **Rocky and Arid Land**:
 
 
• Rocky and arid lands are typically **infertile** and lack sufficient water for agriculture.
 
• These lands are found in regions like the **Thar Desert** in Rajasthan.
 
• Limited agricultural activities are carried out here, primarily depending on **irrigation techniques** and drought-resistant crops.
 
 
 
• **Forest Land**:
 
 
• Forest land is rich in organic matter but is primarily used for **forestry and biodiversity conservation** rather than agriculture.
 
• Clearing forest land for farming can lead to **deforestation and environmental degradation**.
 
• Some tribal communities practice **shifting cultivation** in forested areas, but this is not a sustainable agricultural practice.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Alluvial Soil in India**:
 
 
• Alluvial soils cover about **40% of India's total land area**, making them the most significant agricultural resource.
 
• These soils are classified into two types: **Bhangar** (older alluvium) and **Khadar** (newer alluvium), both of which are highly fertile.
 
• The availability of water from rivers like the Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Yamuna further enhances agricultural productivity in these regions.
 
 
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 
• India's agricultural sector relies heavily on alluvial soil for producing staple crops like **rice and wheat**, which are essential for food security.
 
• Efficient irrigation systems and regular flooding of rivers help maintain the fertility of alluvial lands.
 
• With proper management, alluvial soils can sustain intensive agriculture, supporting India's status as one of the leading producers of various crops globally.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?

__
 
• The **Citizenship Act, 1955** specifies the modes of acquiring Indian citizenship, including **birth, descent, registration, and naturalization**. "By adoption" is not a recognized mode under this Act.
 
• **By birth:** Any individual born in India on or after January 26, 1950, but before July 1, 1987, is an Indian citizen by birth, irrespective of their parents’ citizenship. After July 1, 1987, citizenship by birth requires at least one parent to be an Indian citizen. Hence, this is a valid mode.
 
• **By descent:** Citizenship can be acquired if an individual is born outside India, provided their parent is an Indian citizen at the time of their birth. This mode is valid under the Act.
 
• **By registration:** Certain categories of people, such as Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) residing in India, spouses of Indian citizens, and others, can acquire citizenship through registration under Section 5 of the Act. This is a valid mode as stated in the Act.
 
• **By naturalization:** Foreign nationals who fulfill certain conditions, such as residence in India for a specified period and renunciation of their original citizenship, can acquire Indian citizenship. This is also valid under the Act.
 
• *Hence, the correct answer is **By adoption**, as it is not a recognized mode under the Citizenship Act, 1955.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Citizenship Act, 1955:**

 
 
• Enacted by the Government of India under Article 11 of the Indian Constitution, which grants Parliament the authority to regulate citizenship.
 
• It governs the acquisition and termination of Indian citizenship and provides provisions for naturalization and registration.
 
• Modes of acquiring citizenship include: **birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory**.
 
 
 
• **By birth:**
 
 
• Individuals born in India between January 26, 1950, and July 1, 1987, are automatically Indian citizens by birth.
 
• After July 1, 1987, citizenship by birth requires at least one parent to be an Indian citizen.
 
• From December 3, 2004, an individual born in India must have both parents not classified as illegal migrants to acquire citizenship by birth.
 
 
 
• **By descent:**
 
 
• A person born outside India is considered an Indian citizen if their parent was an Indian citizen at the time of their birth.
 
• Special provisions exist for children born abroad to Indian citizens working for the Government of India.
 
 
 
• **By registration:**
 
 
• Citizenship can be acquired by individuals of Indian origin living in India for a specified period, spouses of Indian citizens, or minors of Indian parents.
 
• The process requires fulfillment of conditions under Section 5 of the Citizenship Act.
 
 
 
• **By naturalization:**
 
 
• Foreign nationals who have resided in India for 12 years (including 1 year immediately before application) and meet other prescribed conditions can acquire citizenship.
 
• The applicant must renounce their previous citizenship and take an oath of allegiance to the Indian Constitution.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Incorporation of Territory:**

 
 
• Citizenship can be granted to individuals of territories that become part of India through political or administrative actions.
 
• For example, individuals in Sikkim became Indian citizens after its incorporation in 1975.
 
 
 
• **Termination of Citizenship:**
 
 
• Citizenship can be terminated under specific conditions such as voluntary acquisition of another country’s citizenship.
 
• It can also be revoked if acquired through fraudulent means.
 
 
 
• **Illegal Migrants:**
 
 
• Individuals who enter India without valid documentation or stay beyond their visa period are classified as illegal migrants and are not eligible for citizenship.
 
• Special provisions under laws like the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 apply to specific communities from neighboring countries.
 
 
 
• **Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA), 2019:**
 
 
• Allows certain persecuted minorities from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and Christians) to apply for Indian citizenship.
 
• Excludes Muslims from these provisions, leading to debates and protests across the country.

questions.question: The Tendulkar Committee revised India's methodology for measuring poverty. As per the Tendulkar Committee, which criterion is considered to measure poverty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Consumption expenditure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Tendulkar Committee**, headed by **Suresh Tendulkar**, was constituted by the Government of India in **2005** to review the methodology for estimating poverty in India.
 
• The committee recommended a shift from the earlier method of measuring poverty based on **calorie intake** to a broader metric based on **consumption expenditure.**
 
• **Consumption expenditure** includes expenses on food, health, education, and other basic needs, providing a more comprehensive measure of poverty.
 
• It also proposed using **implicit price indices** derived from the **National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO)** data to calculate poverty lines, ensuring better alignment with actual consumption patterns.
 
• The Tendulkar methodology was used to estimate poverty lines for both **urban** and **rural areas**, accounting for regional variations in consumption and living standards.
 
• As per the committee's methodology, the national poverty line was set at a monthly per capita expenditure of **₹816** for rural areas and **₹1000** for urban areas in **2004-05.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Calorie Intake:**

 
 
• Earlier methods of poverty estimation, such as those by the Planning Commission, relied heavily on **calorie intake** to define poverty lines.
 
• The calorie-based poverty line focused on providing the minimum required caloric energy—**2400 kcal** for rural areas and **2100 kcal** for urban areas.
 
• However, this approach was criticized for ignoring other essential factors such as **healthcare, education, and housing.**
 
 
 
• **Income:**
 
 
• Income-based poverty measurement focuses on the **earning capacity** of individuals or households.
 
• This metric has limitations as it does not account for **inequalities in consumption** or access to services.
 
• India does not officially use income as the sole criterion for poverty estimation.
 
 
 
• **Employment Status:**
 
 
• While employment status is crucial for understanding economic stability, it is not directly used for poverty estimation in India.
 
• Unemployment or informal employment can contribute to poverty, but measures like the Tendulkar methodology rely on actual **expenditure data** rather than employment data.
 
 
 
• **Key Developments Post-Tendulkar Committee:**
 
 
• The **Rangarajan Committee**, established in **2012**, revised the Tendulkar methodology and adopted a new method for poverty calculation, focusing on **basic needs.**
 
• It updated poverty lines to ₹972 per capita per month for rural areas and ₹1407 for urban areas in **2011-12.**
 
• India's poverty estimation has evolved to include broader metrics like the **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**, which considers factors like health, education, and living standards.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO):**

 
 
• The NSSO, under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, conducts household surveys that are crucial for poverty estimation.
 
• Data from NSSO surveys forms the basis of poverty lines recommended by the Tendulkar and Rangarajan Committees.
 
 
 
• **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):**
 
 
• The MPI, developed by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** and **Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI)**, measures poverty across multiple dimensions.
 
• India's MPI score is based on factors like **health, education, and living standards** instead of income or expenditure alone.

• The **Narmada River** originates from the **Amarkantak Plateau** in the state of **Madhya Pradesh**, India.
 
• It flows in a **westward direction**, making it unique as most rivers in India flow eastward.
 
• The Narmada River is often referred to as the **"Life Line of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat."**
 
• The river flows through the **states of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat** before draining into the **Arabian Sea.**
 
• It is one of the most important rivers of peninsular India and is considered sacred by many communities.

• The Narmada River is a **rift valley river**, flowing between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
 
• It is one of the few rivers in India that flows **from east to west.**
 
• The total length of the river is approximately **1,312 km**, making it one of the longest rivers in India.
 
• The river is known for its unique **marble rocks** at Bhedaghat, near Jabalpur.

• Tagore was a polymath—he excelled as a poet, philosopher, playwright, novelist, and composer, making significant contributions to Indian literature and culture.
 
 
 
• **Translation of Gitanjali:**

• **Significance of Gitanjali:**

• **Other Works of Tagore:**
